title: Shared-state concurrency
summary: Mutex and its lock guard, why Rc fails across threads, Arc for atomic reference counting, Arc<Mutex<T>>, RwLock, atomics, condition variables in brief, deadlocks and poisoning, and the parallels with Rc<RefCell<T>>.

sections: TRPL 16.3 Multiple Ownership with Multiple Threads
TRPL 16.3 Atomic Reference Counting with Arc<T>
PR ch19 What Is a Mutex?
PR ch19 Why Mutexes Are Not Always a Good Idea

blocks.md:
Message passing is one way to cooperate. The other is **shared state**: several threads access the same memory. Channels are like single ownership (a value moves from one owner to the next); shared state is like multiple ownership. Rust's types and ownership make it far less error-prone than in most languages.

The basic tool is a **mutex** (*mutual exclusion*): it lets only one thread at a time access the data. A thread must **lock** the mutex to get access and **unlock** it when done. In many languages forgetting either step is a common bug. In Rust, you cannot get at the data without locking, and unlocking happens automatically.

blocks.explain: `lock()` blocks until the lock is free and returns a `MutexGuard`, a smart pointer to the data: `Deref` gives access, `Drop` releases the lock. The data inside a `Mutex` is only reachable through a guard, so you cannot forget to lock.

blocks.title: Sharing a Mutex between threads
blocks.md: Ten threads should each increment one counter. A first attempt moves the mutex into the first thread, so the second cannot use it. Wrapping it in `Rc` to give it several owners fails too:

blocks.explain: `Rc` updates its count without synchronization. Two threads cloning or dropping at the same moment could corrupt the count and free the data too early or never. The compiler knows `Rc` is not `Send` (lesson 4) and refuses.

blocks.title: Arc<T>
blocks.md: **`Arc<T>`** is the **atomically reference counted** version of `Rc<T>`: it updates the count with atomic CPU instructions that are safe across threads. Atomic operations cost a little more, which is why the standard library does not make every `Rc` atomic. The API is the same:

blocks.explain: `counter` is not `mut`, yet each thread changes the number inside. `Mutex<T>` provides **interior mutability**, like `RefCell<T>`, but safe across threads.

blocks.title: RwLock and atomics
blocks.md:
**`RwLock<T>`** allows **many readers or one writer**, the borrowing rules as a lock: `read()` returns a shared guard, `write()` an exclusive one. It suits data that is read often and changed rarely, such as configuration.

**Atomics** (`std::sync::atomic`) are integers and booleans that threads can update without a lock, using special CPU instructions. They are the fastest option for counters and flags:

blocks.explain: `Ordering` says how the atomic operation is ordered relative to other memory accesses. `Relaxed` is enough for an independent counter; flags that guard other data need `Acquire`/`Release`. *Programming Rust* and the Rustonomicon cover memory ordering in depth; when unsure, `SeqCst` is the safest choice.

blocks.title: Deadlocks and poisoning
blocks.md: Rust prevents data races, not **logic** errors. If thread 1 locks A then B while thread 2 locks B then A, each can wait for the other forever: a **deadlock**. Always acquire several locks in the same order, and hold locks as briefly as possible. If a thread **panics while holding a lock**, the mutex becomes **poisoned**: later `lock()` calls return `Err`, because the data may be half-updated. That is why examples call `.unwrap()` on `lock()`.

blocks.title: A concurrent word counter
blocks.goal: Share a map between threads with Arc<Mutex<...>>, use an atomic counter, and keep locks short.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub fn count_words(texts: Vec<String>, threads: usize) -> (BTreeMap<String, usize>, usize)`: split `texts` among `threads` worker threads (at least 1; text `i` goes to worker `i % threads`). Each worker counts lowercase words (split on whitespace, trim `.,!?;:` from both ends, skip empty) into a **local** `HashMap`, then merges it into one shared `Arc<Mutex<BTreeMap<String, usize>>>` with a single lock. A shared `Arc<AtomicUsize>` counts how many texts were processed. Return the merged map and that count.
- `pub struct Stats { inner: Mutex<Vec<u64>> }` with `pub fn new() -> Stats`, `pub fn record(&self, v: u64)` and `pub fn mean(&self) -> Option<f64>`. Note that `record` takes `&self`: the tests share a `Stats` between scoped threads.
hints: Buckets: `let mut buckets = vec![Vec::new(); w]; for (i, t) in texts.into_iter().enumerate() { buckets[i % w].push(t); }`
Merge with one lock: `let mut map = shared.lock().unwrap(); for (k, v) in local { *map.entry(k).or_insert(0) += v; }`
After joining, take the map out with `Arc::try_unwrap(shared).unwrap().into_inner().unwrap()` or clone it under the lock.
blocks.solution_explain: Counting into a local map and merging once keeps each thread's time under the lock tiny; locking for every word would make the threads queue up behind one another. After all threads are joined, `Arc::try_unwrap` succeeds because only one owner remains, and `into_inner` takes the map out of the mutex without cloning.

points: `Mutex<T>` guards data; `lock()` returns a guard that unlocks when dropped.
`Arc<T>` is the thread-safe `Rc<T>`; `Arc<Mutex<T>>` is shared mutable state across threads.
`RwLock` allows many readers or one writer; atomics update numbers and flags without locks.
Rust prevents data races but not deadlocks: lock in a consistent order and briefly.
A panic while holding a lock poisons the mutex.

terms.def: A lock that allows only one thread at a time to access the data it guards.
The smart pointer returned by lock(); it gives access to the data and releases the lock when dropped.
An atomically reference-counted pointer: Rc that is safe to share between threads.
A lock allowing many simultaneous readers or one writer.
A type whose operations happen indivisibly across threads, without a lock.
A mutex marking itself as possibly inconsistent after a thread panicked while holding it.
A condition variable: lets threads sleep until another thread signals that a condition changed.
